Performance and platforms

Source: vignettes/articles/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd

This page is for readers who want to know what zupmxode costs before they use it: how its compile and solve times compare with rxode2 and mrgsolve on the same machine, and where it runs native code or MIR’s interpreter.

Benchmarks

tools/run-benchmarks in the source repository times each workload of the package’s design (§10) for every engine installed, and keeps every run in .agents/benchmarks.csv. The table shows the latest measured run of each row. “zupmxode/lsoda” is zupmxode made to use LSODA, rxode2’s solver, where it would choose the matrix exponential.

Workload Target zupmxode zupmxode/lsoda rxode2 mrgsolve
Compile a two-compartment model under 20 ms 0.011 0.946 1.67
200 candidate models, compiled and run faster than rxode2 2.59 198 321
Closed form, 1e6 subjects matches rxode2 3.71 39.8 11.1
Two-compartment ODE, 1e3 x 1e3, 1 thread within 1.5x of rxode2 2.86 4.97 1.52 0.765
The same, interpreter tier recorded 3.9 8.11
Seven-cycle antibody workload, obs/s above 5,000 297,900 128,400 289,300 397,700

Times are in seconds, except the last row. They were taken on one Darwin x86_64 Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8500B CPU @ 3.00GHz 6 cores, a machine that was not idle; rxode2’s closed-form row is from an earlier day, when it had the memory that row needs. That build of R has no OpenMP, so every row ran on one thread. The two-compartment ODE misses its target (issue #34); the compile and candidate rows, which a model-building loop pays for, are two orders of magnitude ahead.

Tiers

zupmxode runs a model on one of two tiers: native code generated by MIR, or MIR’s interpreter. Both give the same doubles, which the test suite checks on every model. The interpreter is the fallback where native code cannot be made; in the table above it is about 1.4 times slower with the matrix exponential and 1.6 times with LSODA. pmx_ode_info() names a model’s tier and pmx_ode_tier() changes it.

Both tiers run on every leg of the package’s R CMD check, which a test asserts on each of them:

Leg Tiers
macOS, R-release native and interpreter
Windows, R-release and R-devel native and interpreter
Ubuntu, R-release and R-oldrel native and interpreter
Linux containers, R-devel (clang 23 and the other compilers R CMD check runs on) native and interpreter

Both tiers need memory that is writable and executable. Where the system refuses it (SELinux’s deny_execmem, some hardened containers), neither runs and models cannot be solved; zumir::zumir_info() says why. On macOS, R needs the allow-jit entitlement that CRAN’s build of R has.

Where next

  • Get started shows the functions these figures time.
  • The reference documents pmx_ode_threads(), which sets the number of threads where OpenMP is present.
